prediction.likelyOutcome: Mad Hatter is likely to recover the roughly $19,500 in pre-notice, undisputed unpaid rent essentially as a matter of law, but its bid for the full $130,000 in accelerated rent through December 2018 faces a real and unresolved election-of-remedies defense (did seeking possession terminate the lease?) plus a genuine fact dispute over whether Mad Hatter made reasonable efforts to mitigate by re-letting. Expect partial summary judgment for the landlord on the arrears, denial of full summary judgment on the accelerated component, and a counterclaim that survives to trial but is unlikely to produce tenant damages given the absence of any pled figure and weak causal link to the vacancy.

issues.label: Landlord's Duty to Mitigate / Reasonable Reletting Efforts
Tenant's Counterclaim: Breach of Lease / Good Faith and Fair Dealing

outcome.description: The trial court granted the landlord summary judgment for all twenty months of unpaid rent (May 2017 through December 2018 at $6,500 a month) plus late fees, $133,900 in total, the full amount claimed in the motion; the tenant's remaining counterclaims went to a jury, which found against it. The Mississippi Court of Appeals affirmed (May 18, 2021) and the Supreme Court of Mississippi, on certiorari, affirmed on March 17, 2022, holding the default letters did not terminate the lease, the election-of-remedies and mitigation arguments were waived, and the alleged breaches were immaterial.
outcome.finalNote: Affirmed by the Court of Appeals and, on certiorari, by the Supreme Court of Mississippi.
